**Lingala** (or **Ngala** , Lingala: _Lingála_[Bantu language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bantu_languages "Bantu languages") spoken in the northwest of the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo"), the northern half of the [Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo "Republic of the Congo"), in their capitals, [Kinshasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinshasa "Kinshasa") and [Brazzaville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazzaville "Brazzaville"), and to a lesser degree as a trade language because of emigration in neighbouring [Angola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angola "Angola") or [Central African Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_African_Republic "Central African Republic"). Lingala has 20 million native speakers and is used by another 20 million as a second language, for an approximate total of 40 million speakers.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-e27-1) A significant portion of both Congolese diasporas speaks Lingala in their countries of immigration like [Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium"), [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") or the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congolese_Americans "Congolese Americans").
## History
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lingala&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]
Before 1880, [Bobangi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangi_language "Bangi language") was an important trade language on the western sections of the [Congo River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo_River "Congo River"), between [Stanley Pool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Pool "Stanley Pool") ([Kinshasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinshasa "Kinshasa")) and the confluence of the Congo and [Ubangi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubangi_River "Ubangi River") rivers (Republic of Congo and Democratic Republic of Congo).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-3) When the first Europeans and their West- and East-African troops started founding state posts for the Belgian king along this river section in the early 1880s, they noticed the widespread use and prestige of Bobangi.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-Samarin-4) They attempted to learn it, but only cared to acquire an imperfect knowledge of it, a process that gave rise to a new, strongly restructured variety, called "the trade language", "the language of the river", or "Bobangi-pidgin", among other names.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-6) In 1884, Europeans introduced this restructured variety of Bobangi in the state post [Bangala Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangala_Station "Bangala Station") to communicate with local Congolese, some of whom had second-language knowledge of original Bobangi, and with the Congolese from more remote areas whom missionaries and colonials had been relocating to the station by force.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-7) The _language of the river_ was therefore soon renamed "Bangala", a label the Europeans had since 1876 also been using as a convenient, but erroneous and non-original[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-9)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-Samarin-4) ethnic name for all Congolese of that region.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-10)
Around 1901–2, [CICM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregatio_Immaculati_Cordis_Mariae "Congregatio Immaculati Cordis Mariae") missionaries started a project to "purify" the _Bangala_ language by cleansing it from the "impure", pidginlike features it had acquired when it emerged out of Bobangi in the early 1880s.
> Around and shortly after 1901, a number of both Catholic and Protestant missionaries working in the western and northern Congo Free State, independently of one another but in strikingly parallel terms, judged that Bangala as it had developed out of Bobangi was too "pidgin like", "too poor" a language to function as a proper means of education and evangelization. Each of them set out on a program of massive corpus planning, aimed at actively "correcting" and "enlarging" Bangala from above [...]. One of them was the Catholic missionary Egide De Boeck of the Congregatio Immaculati Cordis Mariae (CICM, commonly known as "the Missionaries of Scheut" or "Scheutists"), who arrived in Bangala Station – Nouvelle Anvers in 1901. Another one was the Protestant missionary Walter H. Stapleton [...], and a third one the Catholic Léon Derikx of the Premonstratensian Fathers [...]. By 1915, De Boeck's endeavors had proven to be more influential than Stapleton's, whose language creative suggestions, as the Protestant missionaries' conference of 1911 admitted, had never been truly implemented [...]. Under the dominance of De Boeck's work, Derikx's discontinued his after less than 10 years.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-11)
Lingala's importance as a [vernacular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernacular "Vernacular") has since grown with the size and importance of its main centers of use, [Kinshasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinshasa "Kinshasa") and [Brazzaville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazzaville "Brazzaville"); with its use as the [lingua franca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingua_franca "Lingua franca") of the armed forces; and with the popularity of [soukous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soukous "Soukous") music.
## Name
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lingala&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Name")]
At first the language the European pioneers and their African troops had forged out of Bobangi was called "the river language", "the trade language", and other volatile names. Beginning in 1884, it was called "Bangala", due to its introduction in [Bangala Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangala_Station "Bangala Station"). After 1901, Catholic missionaries of [CICM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CICM_Missionaries "CICM Missionaries"), also called the Congregation of Scheutists, proposed to rename the language "Lingala". It took some decades for this to be generally accepted both by colonials and the Congolese.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-12) The name _Lingala_ first appears in writing in a 1901-2 publication by the [CICM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CICM_Missionaries "CICM Missionaries") missionary [Égide De Boeck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89gide_de_Boeck "Égide de Boeck").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-13) This name change was accepted in western and northwestern Congo, and in other countries where the language was spoken, but not in northeastern Congo, where the variety of the language spoken locally is still called _[Bangala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangala_language "Bangala language")_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-14)
## Bobangi–Lingala relationship
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lingala&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Bobangi–Lingala relationship")]
Linguistically, Lingala is a dialect or variant of Bobangi, a popular or commercial Bobangi, that is, a Bobangi lingua franca spoken by non-native speakers.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-16) Lingala has also been referred to by the following names: "bad Bobangi",[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-17) "Sabir of Bobangi",[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-18) "deformed and mixed Bobangi",[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-19) "Bobangi of treaties",[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-20) "patois of Bobangi and Kilolo[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-21)", and "the new language of the Bobangi".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-22)
## Characteristics and usage
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lingala&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Characteristics and usage")]
Lingala is a Bantu language of Central Africa[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-23) with roots in the Bobangi language, which provided most of its lexicon and grammar.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-24) In its basic vocabulary, Lingala also borrows from other languages, such as [Kikongo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kikongo "Kikongo") varieties, [Ubangian languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubangian_languages "Ubangian languages"), [Swahili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swahili_language "Swahili language"), [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"), [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language "Portuguese language"), [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language"), and various African languages (note local and foreign interaction with Krumen).
In practice, the extent of borrowing varies widely with speakers of different regions (commonly among young people), and during different occasions.

## Variation
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lingala&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Variation")]
The Lingala language can be divided into several [regiolects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dialect "Dialect") and [sociolects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociolect "Sociolect"). The major regional varieties are northwestern Lingala, Kinshasa Lingala and Brazzaville Lingala.
Literary Lingala (_lingala littéraire_ or _lingala classique_ in French) is a standardized form used mostly in education and news broadcasts on state-owned radio or television and in Roman Catholic religious services, It is taught as a subject at some educational levels. It is historically associated with the work of the Catholic Church, the Belgian [CICM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CICM_Missionaries "CICM Missionaries") missionaries in particular. It has a seven-vowel system (/a/ /e/ /ɛ/ /i/ /o/ /ɔ/ /u/[vowel harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vowel_harmony "Vowel harmony"). It also has a full range of morphological noun prefixes with mandatory grammatical agreement system with subject–verb, or noun–modifier for each of class. It is largely used in formal functions and in some forms of writing. Most native speakers of Spoken Lingala and Kinshasa Lingala consider it incomprehensible.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-27)
Northwestern (or _Equateur_) Lingala is the product of the (incomplete) internalization by Congolese of the prescriptive rules the CICM missionaries intended when designing Literary Lingala.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-29) The northwest is a zone where the CICM missionaries strongly supported the network of schools.
Spoken Lingala (called _lingala parlé_ in French) is the variety mostly used in Lingalaphones' day-to-day lives. It has a full morphological noun prefix system, but the agreement system in the noun phrase is laxer than the literary variety's. There is a five-vowel system and no vowel harmony. Spoken Lingala is largely used in informal functions, and the majority of Lingala songs use spoken Lingala. Modern spoken Lingala is influenced by French; French verbs, for example, may be "lingalized", adding Lingala inflection prefixes and suffixes: "acomprenaki te" or "acomprendraki te" ("he did not understand", using the French word _comprendre_) instead of classic Lingala "asímbaki ntína te" (literally: "s/he grasped/held the root/cause not"). These French influences are more prevalent in Kinshasa and indicate an erosion of the language as education in French becomes accessible to more of the population. There are pronunciation differences between "Catholic Lingala" and "Protestant Lingala", for example nzala/njala ("hunger").
_Lingala ya Bayankee_ (sometimes called _Yanké_) is a sociolect widely used in Kinshasa, e.g., by street youth, street vendors, criminal gangs and homeless children.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lingala#cite_note-30) _Langila_ is a little-studied language game (or ludic practice) musicians initially created shortly after 2000 that is increasingly used in social media and sites of cultural production.

### Tones
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lingala&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Tones")]
Lingala is a [tonal language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonal_language "Tonal language"). Tone is a distinguishing feature in [minimal pairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimal_pair "Minimal pair"), e.g.: _mutu_ (human being) and _mutú_ (head), or kokoma (to write) and kokóma (to arrive). There are two main tones, low and high, and two less common ones: starting high, dipping low, and ending high, all within the same vowel sound, e.g., _mǐso_ (eyes); and starting low, rising high, and ending low, e.g.,  _bôngó_ (therefore).

### Noun class system
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lingala&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Noun class system")]
Akin to all [Bantu languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bantu_languages "Bantu languages"), Lingala has a [noun class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noun_class "Noun class") system in which nouns are classified according to the [prefixes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prefix_\(linguistics\) "Prefix \(linguistics\)") they bear and the prefixes they trigger in sentences. The table below shows Lingala's noun classes ordered according to the numbering system widely used in descriptions of Bantu languages.

Individual classes pair up to form singular/plural pairs, sometimes called genders. There are seven genders. The singular classes 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9 take their plural forms from classes 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, respectively. Additionally, many household items found in class 9 take a class 2 prefix (_ba_) in the plural: _lútu_ → _balútu_ 'spoon', _mésa_ → _bamésa_ 'table', _sáni_ → _basáni_ 'plate'. Words in class 11 usually take a class 10 plural. Most words from class 14 (abstract nouns) do not have a plural counterpart.
Class 9 and 10 have a nasal prefix, which [assimilates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assimilation_\(linguistics\) "Assimilation \(linguistics\)") to the following consonant. Thus, the prefix shows up as 'n' on words that start with _t_ or _d_ , e.g. _ntaba_ 'goat', but as 'm' on words that start with _b_ or _p_ (e.g. _mbísi_ 'fish'). There is also a prefixless class 9a and 10a, exemplified by _sánzá_ → _sánzá_ 'moon(s) or month(s)'. Possible ambiguities are resolved by context.
Noun class prefixes show up not only on the noun itself, but as markers throughout a sentence. In the sentences below, the class prefixes are underlined. (There is a special verbal form 'a' of the prefix for class 1 nouns.)

To a certain extent, noun class allocation is [semantically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semantics "Semantics") governed. Classes 1/2, as in all Bantu languages, mainly contain words for human beings; similarly, classes 9/10 contain many words for animals. In other classes, semantical regularities are mostly absent or obscured by many exceptions.
### Verb inflections and morphology
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lingala&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Verb inflections and morphology")]
#### Verbal extensions
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lingala&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Verbal extensions")]
Four morphemes modify verbs. They are added to a verb root in the following order:
  1. Reversive (-ol-)     e.g.: kozinga _to wrap_ and kozingola _to develop_
  2. Causative (-is-)     e.g. : koyéba _to know_ and koyébisa _to inform_
  3. Applicative (-el-)     e.g. : kobíka _to heal (self), to save (self)_ and kobíkela _to heal (someone else), to save (someone)_
  4. Passive (-am-)     e.g. : koboma _to kill_ and kobomama _to be killed_
  5. Reciprocal or stationary (-an-, sometimes -en-)     e.g. : kokúta _to find_ and kokútana _to meet_


#### Tense inflections
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lingala&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Tense inflections")]
The first tone segment affects the subject part of the verb; the second attaches to the semantic morpheme attached to its root.
  * present perfect (LH-í)
  * simple present (LL-a)
  * recurrent present (LL-aka)
  * undefined recent past (LH-ákí)
  * undefined distant past (LH-áká)
  * future (L-ko-L-a)
  * subjunctive (HL-a)


## Writing system
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lingala&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Writing system")]
Lingala is more a spoken than a written language, and has several different writing systems, most of them ad hoc. As literacy in Lingala tends to be low, its popular orthography is very flexible and varies among the two republics. Some orthographies are heavily influenced by French; influences include a double S, _ss_ , to transcribe [s] (in the Republic of the Congo); _ou_ for [u] (in the Republic of the Congo); i with trema, _aï_ , to transcribe [áí][aí]_é_ , to transcribe [e]; _e_ to transcribe [ɛ][ɔ][ɔ]_sango_ is an alternative to _nsango_ (information or news); _nyonso_ , _nyoso_ , _nionso_ , _nioso_ (every) are all transcriptions of _nyɔ́nsɔ_.
In 1976, the _Société Zaïroise des Linguistes_ ([Zairian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zaire "Zaire") Linguists Society) adopted a writing system for Lingala, using the open e (ɛ)(ɔ)[ɛ][ɔ]ɛɔ
The popular orthographies are often more simplified and ambiguous than the academic-based ones. Many Lingala books, papers, the translation of the [Universal Declaration of Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Declaration_of_Human_Rights "Universal Declaration of Human Rights"), Internet forums, newsletters, and major websites such as Google's Lingala do not use the Lingala-specific characters ɛ and ɔ. Tone marking is found in most literary works.

### Mandombe

The [Mandombe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandombe "Mandombe") script is an [abugida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abugida "Abugida"), primarily used to write [Kikongo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kikongo "Kikongo"), that can also be used for Lingala.
